profiles.meeting_scenario: The Pediatric Device Consortia team is holding a design review of a near-final scoping review protocol on barriers to and facilitators of paediatric medical device clinical research before launching screening in Covidence and updating the OSF record. The meeting is between the clinical principal investigator and the evidence-synthesis lead to evaluate whether the current protocol wording, screening workflow, and data-charting structure are sufficiently complete for operational use. The agenda is to review the inclusion language for paediatric studies, confirm what counts as an infrastructural barrier or facilitator during extraction, and verify the reviewer conflict-resolution workflow. The expected outcome is a shared decision that the protocol is ready for pilot screening next week with only minor wording edits.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rios
members.role: Clinical Principal Investigator, Pediatric Device Consortia
members.expertise: Paediatric cardiology, investigator-initiated device trials, multicentre clinical research operations
members.background: Dr. Rios is a paediatric cardiologist who has led several early-feasibility and postmarket device studies involving congenital heart disease populations and now oversees the consortium's clinical research strategy.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol approved quickly so the team can begin screening before the next consortium progress report, and she is especially concerned that the review not become so methodologically narrow that it misses practical obstacles trial teams actually face.
hidden_assumptions: A study can still count as paediatric-focused if it includes mixed-age participants so long as children are a meaningful subgroup or the device is clearly intended for paediatric use.

Infrastructural barriers include frontline study-conduct problems such as consent burden, low case volume, and site recruitment friction, because those are manifestations of weak research infrastructure.
When the protocol says the PI resolves conflicts, that refers to adjudicating only explicit include-versus-exclude disagreements after independent reviewer decisions are entered.
If the broad concept is captured correctly in the protocol, operational details can be handled pragmatically during screening without needing tighter specification now.

members.name: Elena Park
members.role: Evidence Synthesis Lead and Health Sciences Information Specialist
members.expertise: Scoping review methods, database searching, Covidence workflow design, reproducible review operations
members.background: Elena Park is a medical librarian and evidence-synthesis specialist who supports clinical review teams across the institution and has implemented screening and charting workflows for multiple scoping and systematic reviews.
members.private_state: She wants a protocol that will produce reproducible reviewer decisions and a clean extraction set, and she is worried that ambiguous wording will create avoidable inconsistency once junior reviewers start screening.
hidden_assumptions: A study is only paediatric-focused for inclusion purposes if paediatric participants are clearly separable in the sample or analysis, rather than simply implied by device intent.

Infrastructure should be coded as system-level research supports or constraints such as networks, funding mechanisms, regulatory pathways, staffing models, and data systems, not generic trial difficulties.
When the protocol says the PI resolves conflicts, the PI should also review uncertain edge cases and classification ambiguities so reviewer practice stays calibrated.
If a concept is not bounded operationally in the protocol, it should be implemented conservatively so screening remains reproducible across reviewers.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a paediatric-focused study
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to including 'paediatric-focused studies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes mixed-age studies can be included when the device is intended for children or when a paediatric subgroup is substantively present, even if paediatric results are not cleanly separated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes inclusion requires a clearly paediatric-only sample or paediatric findings that are separately identifiable enough for consistent reviewer judgment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants strongly endorse the same inclusion aim and use the same phrase, and because they are discussing protocol readiness rather than adjudicating an actual borderline paper, each assumes the other shares their threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of infrastructural barriers and facilitators
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the extraction should capture 'infrastructural barriers and facilitators.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats any recurring obstacle or enabler of running paediatric device studies as infrastructure, including recruitment difficulty, parental consent complexity, low site volume, and sponsor hesitancy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 limits infrastructure to underlying research-system capacities and supports, such as trial networks, funding programs, ethics/regulatory processes, staffing, and data platforms; study-level difficulties can be noted but are outside the main coding frame.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds naturally broad and mission-aligned, and M2's mention of noting other issues in comments makes it appear that nothing important is being excluded even though the formal extraction scope differs.

misalignment_points.topic: How PI conflict resolution will operate
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that 'the PI will resolve conflicts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes only direct reviewer disagreements at title/abstract or full-text decision points will be escalated to him for occasional adjudication.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the PI will also routinely review uncertain or ambiguous records during the pilot and early screening so edge-case interpretation stays standardized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The workflow phrase is standard in review protocols, so both hear it as settled language; each silently fills in the operational details from prior experience and neither sees a reason to unpack them in a brief readiness meeting.

turns.inner_thought: I need this protocol over the line so we can start screening before the consortium update, but I do not want the review boxed into such a narrow methods frame that it ignores what trial teams actually run into on the ground. For me, infrastructural barriers and facilitators absolutely include the day-to-day things that make pediatric device studies hard to execute, like consent burden, low volume, and site activation friction. If we miss those, the review will sound tidy and useless.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mostly want to confirm we're genuinely ready to launch and that the review will still capture the real barriers teams face in paediatric device studies. As long as the protocol and forms leave room for infrastructural barriers and facilitators in a way that reflects actual study conduct, I think we're close.

turns.inner_thought: Searches are almost finalized, Covidence is configured, and the main risk now is preventable inconsistency once junior reviewers start screening. The two places ambiguity will bite us are paediatric-focused studies and how the PI will resolve conflicts. I want those handled tightly enough that decisions are reproducible without creating cleanup problems later.
turns.utterance: From my side, we're nearly there. The database strategies are in good shape, and the Covidence project is basically set up. What I'd like to sanity-check today is the inclusion wording around paediatric-focused studies and just make sure the reviewer workflow is clear, especially that the PI will resolve conflicts.

turns.inner_thought: If a paper is about a device intended for children, or if children are a meaningful part of the study population, that is exactly the kind of literature we need. I do not need separate pediatric-only tables in every paper for it to be informative. I assume Elena means the same broad, clinically sensible standard when she says paediatric-focused studies.
turns.utterance: On the inclusion side, I think we should keep the spirit fairly straightforward. If a paper is clearly centered on a device for children or is otherwise obviously relevant to paediatric care, it still reads to me as paediatric-focused studies for this review.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as reviewers can see the pediatric relevance in the title, abstract, or population description and make the same call consistently. In practice, I will still want the pilot to lean conservative where the pediatric sample is not clearly separable, but I don't need to spell that out if the wording stays at the level of paediatric-focused studies.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's workable. As long as the paediatric relevance is clear from the study aim and population description, reviewers should be able to handle paediatric-focused studies consistently during screening.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Now I need to be sure the charting won't wash out the practical obstacles. For this topic, infrastructural barriers and facilitators should definitely include hard consent processes, low case volume, site recruitment challenges, and sponsor hesitation, because those are exactly how weak infrastructure shows up in pediatric device research.
turns.utterance: The other piece I care about is the charting form. I want it to leave enough room for infrastructural barriers and facilitators that show up in the way these studies actually get done, because otherwise we'll miss what slows paediatric trials down in practice.

turns.inner_thought: My extraction framework is already organized around system-level infrastructure: funding, site capacity, ethics and regulatory processes, staffing, data supports, networks. If papers mention more local operational hassles, we can still preserve them in notes, but I don't want the main coding frame to become an unbounded list of generic trial problems.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. In the draft framework, the main extraction fields already cover infrastructural barriers and facilitators across domains like funding, site capacity, ethics and regulatory processes, and staffing. If other practical issues come up in the papers, we can capture those in notes so they aren't lost.

turns.inner_thought: As long as disagreements don't clog the timeline, I'm happy. When I say the PI will resolve conflicts, I mean once the two reviewers have independently made their include/exclude calls and there is a direct disagreement, they can send it to me and I'll adjudicate quickly. I am not planning to sit in weekly calibration on every fuzzy record.
turns.utterance: Great. And on workflow, I think we can keep it simple: once the two reviewers disagree on a record, the PI will resolve conflicts so the queue keeps moving and screening doesn't stall.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll build the pilot and early screening around regular PI review of disagreements and uncertain edge cases so we keep interpretation aligned from the start. When I hear that the PI will resolve conflicts, that includes the ambiguous records we use for calibration, not just clean yes-versus-no splits.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll set it up so that after the pilot we can queue the uncertain records for weekly PI review as part of that, and the PI will resolve conflicts so reviewer practice stays calibrated before we scale up.

turns.inner_thought: Weekly review is fine if it's light-touch, but I mainly want us moving next week. The form should stay lean; we do not need a huge coding schema that slows abstraction. If the broad concepts are in place, the team can handle edge cases pragmatically during screening and we can still get to a useful narrative synthesis.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. If the pilot looks smooth, I'd like us to move straight into full screening next week. And I'd prefer to keep the REDCap charting form fairly lean so we're not overbuilding it when the goal is an efficient narrative synthesis.

turns.inner_thought: I can make a few wording refinements now, keep the protocol operationally conservative where needed, and finalize the pilot set in Covidence. From my perspective, we're ready as long as the protocol text signals paediatric-focused studies, infrastructural barriers and facilitators, and that the PI will resolve conflicts. The rest I can standardize through the pilot.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll make a few wording refinements, finalize the pilot set in Covidence, and update the OSF-facing version accordingly. Barring anything unexpected, I'll mark the protocol as ready to proceed.
